title: Berkshire 1989 letter: Cigar butts vs wonderful businesses, float-backed risk taking, and a no-leverage temperament
summary: Buffett's 1989 letter defines intrinsic value, explains why high growth rates fade as the base grows, and lays out the economics of deferred taxes and look-through earnings. His "Mistakes of the First Twenty-five Years" covers cigar-butt investing, the institutional imperative, and refusing leverage. He also explains why Berkshire writes insurance only at profitable prices.

principles.text: Intrinsic value is all future cash flows discounted at prevailing interest rates, which makes all businesses economic equals.
principles.quote: With perfect foresight, this number can be calculated by taking all future cash flows of a business - in and out - and discounting them at prevailing interest rates.

principles.text: Buy a wonderful company at a fair price rather than a fair company at a wonderful price.
principles.quote: It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price.

principles.text: Cigar-butt bargains disappoint because low business returns erode the initial discount; time favors great businesses.
principles.quote: Time is the friend of the wonderful business, the enemy of the mediocre.

principles.text: Avoid leverage: a small chance of ruin is not worth a large chance of extra returns.
principles.quote: A small chance of distress or disgrace cannot, in our view, be offset by a large chance of extra returns.

principles.text: Take rational risks others avoid, indifferent to reported quarterly results, when aligned with owners.
principles.quote: We are willing to look foolish as long as we don't feel we have acted foolishly.

principles.text: Only partner with people you like, trust and admire; bad people don't make good deals.
principles.quote: We've never succeeded in making a good deal with a bad person.
